# Live Replication in Amazon S3

## Overview

Live replication is the automatic, asynchronous copying of objects across general purpose buckets in the same or different AWS Regions. It copies newly created objects and object updates from a source bucket to a destination bucket or buckets. When you configure replication, you add replication rules to the source bucket. These rules define which source bucket objects to replicate and the destination bucket or buckets where the replicated objects are stored. You can create a rule to replicate all the objects in a bucket or a subset of objects with a specific key name prefix, one or more object tags, or both. A destination bucket can be in the same AWS account as the source bucket, or it can be in a different account.

The number of destination buckets is limited to the number of AWS Regions in a given partition. AWS currently has three partitions: aws, aws-cn, and aws-us-gov.

If you specify an object version ID to delete, Amazon S3 deletes that object version in the source bucket but does not replicate the deletion in the destination bucket. Not replicating version-specific deletions to the destination protects data from malicious deletions.

## Creating a Replication Rule

When you add a replication rule to a bucket, the rule is enabled by default, so it starts working as soon as you save it. After saving a rule, you can edit, enable, disable, or delete it.

The replication rule name is required and must be unique within the bucket. If the bucket has existing replication rules, you must set a priority for the rule to avoid conflicts caused by objects in the scope of more than one rule. In the case of overlapping rules, Amazon S3 uses the rule priority to determine which rule to apply, and the higher the number, the higher the priority. If you enter a prefix that is the name of a folder, you must use / (forward slash) as the last character.

If versioning is not enabled on the destination bucket, the console shows a warning with an Enable versioning button.

Unless you choose to change the storage class, the storage class for replicated objects is the same as the original objects.

When you use S3 RTC or S3 Replication metrics, additional fees apply.

## IAM Role and Permissions

When you add a replication rule to a bucket, you must have the iam:PassRole permission to pass the IAM role that grants Amazon S3 replication permissions. If you choose an existing IAM role, you must choose a role that grants Amazon S3 the necessary permissions for replication. Replication fails if the IAM role does not grant Amazon S3 sufficient permissions to follow your replication rule. Choosing Create new role has Amazon S3 generate a policy for the IAM role matching the chosen source and destination buckets, and is highly recommended.

If you want to replicate encrypted objects, you must also grant the necessary AWS KMS key permissions. To use Object Lock with replication, you must grant s3:GetObjectRetention and s3:GetObjectLegalHold on the source S3 bucket in the IAM role used to set up replication. If the role has an s3:Get* permission statement, that statement satisfies the Object Lock permission requirement. To replicate object annotations, you must also grant s3:GetObjectVersionAnnotationForReplication on the source bucket in the IAM role permissions policy.

If the destination bucket is in a different account from the source bucket, you must add a bucket policy to the destination bucket to grant the owner of the source bucket account permission to replicate objects.

## Replicating Objects Encrypted with AWS KMS

When you replicate objects encrypted with AWS KMS, the AWS KMS request rate doubles in the source Region and increases in the destination Region by the same amount. If your current PUT object request rate during replication is more than half the default AWS KMS rate limit, AWS recommends requesting an increase to your AWS KMS request rate quota.

You can only use KMS keys that are enabled in the same AWS Region as the bucket. The S3 console lists only 100 KMS keys per Region, so keys beyond the first 100 require entering the KMS key ARN. Amazon S3 supports only symmetric encryption KMS keys and not asymmetric KMS keys.

## Using the AWS CLI for Same-Account Replication

To use the AWS CLI for same-account replication, you create buckets, enable versioning, create an IAM role, add the replication configuration to the source bucket, and then test. For same-account replication, the same profile is used for the source and destination buckets. Specifying the IAM role in the replication configuration requires that the profile used has the iam:PassRole permission. The trust policy grants the Amazon S3 service principal permission to assume the role via sts:AssumeRole.

The Amazon S3 API requires the replication configuration as XML, whereas the AWS CLI requires it as JSON. The example rule replicates objects with the Tax prefix except objects under Tax/drafts/.

## Verifying Replication

The time it takes Amazon S3 to replicate an object depends on the size of the object. Replicas in the destination bucket should have Replication status REPLICA and be owned by the source bucket account. When source and destination buckets are owned by different accounts, Amazon S3 can be configured to change replica ownership to the destination account.

# Live Replication in Amazon S3

## Overview

Live replication is the automatic, asynchronous copying of objects across general purpose buckets in the same or different AWS Regions. It copies newly created objects and object updates from a source bucket to a destination bucket or buckets. A destination bucket can be in the same AWS account as the source bucket, or in a different account. The number of destination buckets is limited to the number of AWS Regions in a given partition. AWS currently has three partitions: aws, aws-cn, and aws-us-gov.

When you configure replication, you add replication rules to the source bucket. These rules define which source bucket objects to replicate and the destination bucket or buckets where the replicated objects are stored. You can create a rule to replicate all the objects in a bucket, or a subset of objects with a specific key name prefix, one or more object tags, or both. When you add a replication rule to a bucket, the rule is enabled by default, so it starts working as soon as you save it. After saving a rule, you can edit, enable, disable, or delete it.

If you specify an object version ID to delete, Amazon S3 deletes that object version in the source bucket but does not replicate the deletion in the destination bucket. Not replicating version-specific deletions protects data from malicious deletions.

## Configuring a rule

The replication rule name is required and must be unique within the bucket. If the bucket has existing replication rules, you must set a priority for the rule to avoid conflicts caused by objects in the scope of more than one rule. In the case of overlapping rules, Amazon S3 uses the rule priority to determine which rule to apply, and the higher the number, the higher the priority. If you enter a prefix that is the name of a folder, you must use / (forward slash) as the last character.

If versioning is not enabled on the destination bucket, the console shows a warning with an Enable versioning button.

If you don't choose to change the storage class, the storage class for replicated objects is the same as the original objects. When you use S3 RTC or S3 Replication metrics, additional fees apply.

## Permissions and IAM role

When you add a replication rule to a bucket, you must have the iam:PassRole permission to pass the IAM role that grants Amazon S3 replication permissions. If you choose an existing IAM role, you must choose a role that grants Amazon S3 the necessary permissions for replication. Replication fails if the IAM role does not grant Amazon S3 sufficient permissions to follow your replication rule. Choosing Create new role has Amazon S3 generate a policy for the IAM role matching the chosen source and destination buckets, and is highly recommended.

To use Object Lock with replication, you must grant s3:GetObjectRetention and s3:GetObjectLegalHold on the source S3 bucket in the IAM role used to set up replication. If the role has an s3:Get* permission statement, that statement satisfies the Object Lock permission requirement. To replicate object annotations, you must also grant s3:GetObjectVersionAnnotationForReplication on the source bucket in the IAM role permissions policy.

If the destination bucket is in a different account from the source bucket, you must add a bucket policy to the destination bucket to grant the owner of the source bucket account permission to replicate objects.

## Replicating encrypted objects

If you want to replicate encrypted objects, you must also grant the necessary AWS KMS key permissions. When you replicate objects encrypted with AWS KMS, the AWS KMS request rate doubles in the source Region and increases in the destination Region by the same amount. If your current PUT object request rate during replication is more than half the default AWS KMS rate limit, AWS recommends requesting an increase to your AWS KMS request rate quota.

You can only use KMS keys that are enabled in the same AWS Region as the bucket. The S3 console lists only 100 KMS keys per Region, so keys beyond the first 100 require entering the KMS key ARN. Amazon S3 supports only symmetric encryption KMS keys and not asymmetric KMS keys.

## Using the AWS CLI for same-account replication

To use the AWS CLI for same-account replication, you create buckets, enable versioning, create an IAM role, add the replication configuration to the source bucket, and then test. For same-account replication, the same profile is used for the source and destination buckets. Specifying the IAM role in the replication configuration requires that the profile used has the iam:PassRole permission. The role's trust policy grants the Amazon S3 service principal permission to assume the role via sts:AssumeRole.

The Amazon S3 API requires the replication configuration as XML, whereas the AWS CLI requires it as JSON. The example rule replicates objects with the Tax prefix except objects under Tax/drafts/.

## Verifying replication

The time it takes Amazon S3 to replicate an object depends on the size of the object. Replicas in the destination bucket should have Replication status REPLICA and be owned by the source bucket account. When source and destination buckets are owned by different accounts, Amazon S3 can be configured to change replica ownership to the destination account.

# Configuring live replication

Live replication is the automatic, asynchronous copying of objects across general purpose buckets in the same or different AWS Regions. It copies newly created objects and object updates from a source bucket to a destination bucket or buckets.

## Before you begin

- **A destination S3 bucket to receive replicated objects.** The bucket must exist before you configure replication. Versioning must be enabled on both the destination bucket and the source bucket. No steps are given here for creating the bucket.
- **Replication permissions for the source and destination buckets.** Set up an IAM role with permissions that Amazon S3 can assume to replicate objects. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/setting-repl-config-perm-overview.html
- **The iam:PassRole permission** for the user adding the replication rule, so that the user can pass the replication role to S3. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_roles_use_passrole.html
- **AWS KMS key permissions, and a destination KMS key, only if you are replicating SSE-KMS encrypted objects.** Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/replication-config-for-kms-objects.html
- **Additional s3:GetObjectRetention and s3:GetObjectLegalHold permissions, only if you use Object Lock.** Grant them on the source bucket in the replication IAM role. Steps: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lock-managing.html

## How replication rules work

When you configure replication, you add replication rules to the source bucket. The rules define which source bucket objects to replicate and the destination bucket or buckets where the replicated objects are stored. You can create a rule that replicates all the objects in a bucket, or a subset of objects with a specific key name prefix, one or more object tags, or both. The example rule in this documentation replicates objects with the Tax prefix except objects under Tax/drafts/.

A destination bucket can be in the same AWS account as the source bucket or in a different account. If the destination bucket is in a different account, you must add a bucket policy to the destination bucket that grants the owner of the source bucket account permission to replicate objects. Amazon S3 can also be configured to change replica ownership to the destination account when the source and destination buckets are owned by different accounts.

The number of destination buckets is limited to the number of AWS Regions in a given partition. AWS currently has three partitions: aws, aws-cn, and aws-us-gov.

When you add a replication rule to a bucket, the rule is enabled by default, so it starts working as soon as you save it. After saving a rule, you can edit, enable, disable, or delete it.

If you specify an object version ID to delete, Amazon S3 deletes that object version in the source bucket but does not replicate the deletion in the destination bucket. Not replicating version-specific deletions protects data from malicious deletions.

## Rule settings

The replication rule name is required and must be unique within the bucket. If the bucket has existing replication rules, you must set a priority for the new rule to avoid conflicts caused by objects in the scope of more than one rule. Setting the priority is enough to resolve overlap: in the case of overlapping rules, Amazon S3 uses the rule priority to determine which rule to apply, and the higher the number, the higher the priority. If you enter a prefix that is the name of a folder, you must use / (forward slash) as the last character.

If versioning is not enabled on the destination bucket, the console shows a warning with an Enable versioning button. If you don't choose to change the storage class, the storage class for replicated objects is the same as the original objects. When you use S3 RTC or S3 Replication metrics, additional fees apply.

## IAM role

When you add a replication rule to a bucket, you must have the iam:PassRole permission to pass the IAM role that grants Amazon S3 replication permissions. If you use the AWS CLI, specifying the IAM role in the replication configuration requires that the profile used has the iam:PassRole permission, and having that permission on the profile is enough to satisfy this requirement.

If you choose an existing IAM role, you must choose a role that grants Amazon S3 the necessary permissions for replication. Replication fails if the IAM role does not grant Amazon S3 sufficient permissions to follow your replication rule; this failure occurs only when the role is passed with iam:PassRole and is an existing role you chose. Choosing Create new role has Amazon S3 generate a policy for the IAM role matching the chosen source and destination buckets, and is highly recommended. The trust policy grants the Amazon S3 service principal permission to assume the role via sts:AssumeRole.

To use Object Lock with replication, you must grant s3:GetObjectRetention and s3:GetObjectLegalHold on the source S3 bucket in the IAM role used to set up replication. If the role has an s3:Get* permission statement, that statement satisfies the Object Lock permission requirement. To replicate object annotations, you must also grant s3:GetObjectVersionAnnotationForReplication on the source bucket in the IAM role permissions policy.

## Encrypted objects

If you want to replicate encrypted objects, you must also grant the necessary AWS KMS key permissions. When you replicate objects encrypted with AWS KMS, the AWS KMS request rate doubles in the source Region and increases in the destination Region by the same amount. If your current PUT object request rate during replication is more than half the default AWS KMS rate limit, AWS recommends requesting an increase to your AWS KMS request rate quota.

You can only use KMS keys that are enabled in the same AWS Region as the bucket. The S3 console lists only 100 KMS keys per Region, so for keys beyond the first 100 you must enter the KMS key ARN. Amazon S3 supports only symmetric encryption KMS keys and not asymmetric KMS keys.

## Using the AWS CLI for same-account replication

To use the AWS CLI for same-account replication, you create buckets, enable versioning, create an IAM role, add the replication configuration to the source bucket, and then test. For same-account replication, the same profile is used for the source and destination buckets. The Amazon S3 API requires the replication configuration as XML, whereas the AWS CLI requires it as JSON.

## Verifying replication

Only after you have completed these configuration steps can you verify the result. The time it takes Amazon S3 to replicate an object depends on the size of the object. Replicas in the destination bucket should have Replication status REPLICA and be owned by the source bucket account.
